newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline dive forces outright U.S. crudes lower.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline dive forces outright U.S. crudes lower.

text.p: Cash crudes in the U.S. Gulf swooned Thursday on carryover pressure generated by weak unleaded gasoline futures, when NYMEX expiry caused a flood of speculative selling, traders said.
September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing talked late some 15 cents lower at $20.10-20 a barrel, with September/October spreads tighter than in the morning at minus 4-6 cents.
Grade business in the Gulf remained stuck at well-established ranges, with deals done at premiums of 25-27 cents for Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James barrels.
West Texas Sour/Midland prices stayed at discounts of $1.35-1.40, and WTI/Cushing Postings Plus around $1.95-2.00.
"There really wasn't much to move prices, and the outright volatility kept people jumpy," said a trader.
Brent/WTI spreads ranged around $1.20 in favor of September WTI, and $1.30 for October.

Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) said a fire at its 310,000 barrels per day (bpd) Curacao refinery forced sharp production cuts. Crude oil throughput was to return to 105,000 bpd within two days. The largest crude distillation tower at the plant was struck by a fire on Thursday morning.

Cano Limon field operator Occidental Petroleum Corp said a Colombian rebel bombing forced closure of the country's main pipeline, halting throughput until repairs were made. The blast did not impact Cano field output, and the pipeline repairs were expected to be completed by late Friday.
On the Iraq front, U.N. officials said late Thursday that completion of the review process for Baghdad's aid distribution plan would likely occur on Monday.
A computer diskette sent as part of the aid plan annex package contained a virus, forcing a delay until a new diskette was sent from Baghdad.
Other minor issues have been settled, the U.N. said, setting the stage for Secretary-General Kofi Annan's okay.

Crude traders said Bayoil and Coastal were heard on the prowl for vessels to lift Iraqi crude for the first 10 days of August, furthering expectations for a quick return of Iraqi exports, once the aid plan meets approval.

"Both have been shopping for crude carriers in the first five to seven days of August. They were both very proud to be first to load last time (the first round of the oil-for-food accord), so I expect this means we are not far away," said a crude trader in the U.S. Gulf.
